subject: Banking
title: Dodd-Frank and Too Big to Fail
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Dodd-Frank and Too Big to Fail.

hook.text: After 2008, Congress passed Dodd-Frank: 2,300 pages of rules designed to prevent banks from crashing the economy again.

buildup.text: The law created stress tests, higher capital requirements, and the Volcker Rule banning risky proprietary trading.

discovery.text: Dodd-Frank also created the CFPB to protect consumers from predatory lending and hidden fees.

twist.text: Critics say Dodd-Frank made banks safer but also harder to access. Small banks struggled with compliance costs.

climax.text: Regulation after every crisis follows the same pattern: dramatic reform, gradual rollback, then the next crisis.

punchline.text: 2,300 pages of rules. The question is whether they survive until the next crash.

quiz.question: What did the Volcker Rule in Dodd-Frank prohibit?
options: Banks making risky proprietary trades with depositor money

details.summary: The Dodd-Frank Act of 2010 was designed to end too-big-to-fail by requiring large banks to hold more capital, submit living wills, and accept new oversight. Fifteen years later, debate continues over whether it actually solved the problem.
details.whyItMatters: Dodd-Frank was the most significant banking reform since the 1930s. Its success or failure in preventing future bailouts determines whether taxpayers are still implicitly backing Wall Street's biggest bets.
takeaways: Dodd-Frank created the Financial Stability Oversight Council to monitor systemic risk
Living wills require banks to plan their own orderly resolution
The 2023 bank failures tested Dodd-Frank's framework in real time

faq.question: Did Dodd-Frank actually end too-big-to-fail?
faq.answer: The 2023 bank failures suggest not entirely. While Dodd-Frank strengthened the system with higher capital requirements and resolution planning, regulators still intervened to protect all depositors, suggesting the implicit government backstop remains.

faq.question: What was the 2018 rollback of Dodd-Frank?
faq.answer: The Economic Growth Act raised the threshold for enhanced supervision from $50 billion to $250 billion in assets. This exempted mid-sized banks like SVB from stricter oversight, which critics argue contributed to the 2023 failures.
